URL: https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/politics/myanmar-uk-sanctions-genocide-rohingya-b3090187.html
The Independent, 23 Nov 2026

Ed Miliband says new laws will also be passed to stop the supply of aviation fuel to the country

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The UK has sanctioned Myanmar’s president and members of the country’s military after the International Criminal Court’s ruling that it had carried out a genocide on the Rohingya people.

Restrictions will be placed on President Min Aung Hlaing and four other senior military members from the country, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said.

New legislation will also be passed to stop the supply of aviation fuel to the country, which was known as Burma until 1989.

Last week, Mr Miliband expelled Myanmar’s defence attache after the UN’s top court ruled that the country had committed genocide during a brutal 2017 military campaign.

He told MPs on Monday that the UK would raise the issue at the UN Security Council this week, and there would be a dedicated meeting in a fortnight.

Speaking in the Commons, Mr Miliband said: “On Thursday, we ordered the expulsion of Myanmar’s defence attache, because we will not tolerate a serving representative of Myanmar’s military remaining imposed on UK soil.

“I can announce today that we have also imposed sanctions against four major generals and a brigadier general, senior military figures who oversaw troops that carried out egregious civilian killings and repression of the population across Myanmar.

“We know also that the Myanmar military has systematically used lethal air power against its own people. I do not believe the British people want any UK companies to have any links to such practices.

“So we will also introduce new legislation in the coming months to stop the export and supply of aviation fuel to Myanmar, which is used in such horrendous attacks.”

Mr Miliband also announced £3 million to help Rohingya survivors, and a further £5 million of humanitarian assistance to support 350,000 Rohingya and Rakhine people.

He said that those affected were struggling to access clean water and were suffering from malnourishment.

In the ruling last week, the ICJ found about 10,000 Rohingya were murdered during the clearance operation in the western Rakhine state that borders Bangladesh and the Bay of Bengal.

Reports included that entire villages were burnt down, and that women and girls were raped.

Mr Miliband said that more than 1.2 million refugees fled and were being supported by Bangladesh.

Myanmar’s leader during the genocide, Aung San Suu Kyi, who studied in England, was deposed by Myanmar’s military in 2021.

MPs heard that air strikes and violence from the Arakan army were still happening.

Mr Miliband said: “For this government, and I would argue for the whole international community, our response to a crime as profoundly shocking as genocide must reflect our values and must be matched by clear action.

“We should also act cognisant of the fact that the appalling targeting of civilians by the Myanmar regime continues to this day, as does the discrimination and persecution of Rohingya and other communities.”

He called for an “immediate pause in hostilities to enable humanitarian aid to get through, a stop to air strikes on civilians, and the release of political prisoners, as well as dialogue towards an inclusive political settlement”.

Mr Miliband said: “Myanmar must stop ongoing violations, investigate, prosecute and punish perpetrators, and prevent such an atrocity from ever happening again.”

He continued: “In the weeks and months ahead, I promise the House the UK will do everything we can to reinvigorate the political and diplomatic efforts to secure a just and lasting end to this appalling conflict.”

Shadow foreign minister Wendy Morton condemned the atrocities committed against the Rohingya, but warned against the “weaponisation” of international law, adding: “We cannot allow legal standards to become subordinate to political objectives.”

She added: “This, as the foreign secretary has set out, is the first time the ICJ has found a state directly responsible for committing genocide.

“Yet the court divided nine to six on that central finding. So it does concern me greatly that the dissenting judges raised substantial questions about proof of intent, the standard of proof, and the treatment of evidence.”

Mr Miliband said: “It is a majority view, but a majority view is the view of the court, just like it would be in our court and, therefore, I do deeply regret her seeking to, if you like, unpick this judgment.”

Labour’s Dame Emily Thornberry, the chair of the Foreign Affairs Committee, said the Conservatives had reached “a new low”, and Liberal Democrat international development spokeswoman Monica Harding said the comments “saddened” her.
